claims.text: The baseline is an equiatomic refractory high-entropy alloy consisting of a single-phase BCC solid solution without significant second-phase precipitation.
A small off-stoichiometric addition of a lightweight element such as Al can trigger ordered L21 precipitation in the BCC alloy during consolidation.
The resulting L21 precipitates will be 10–30 nm in size and homogeneously dispersed in the BCC matrix.
Ordered L21 precipitates will impede dislocation motion and provide precipitation strengthening.
The L21 precipitates will strengthen the alloy through load transfer.
The modified alloy will have approximately 15–20% higher yield strength than the baseline at 600–700 °C.
The proposed high-temperature capability is intended to hold under compressive loading at 600–700 °C.
Temperatures of 600–700 °C are typical jet-turbine operating conditions.
The compositional modification will maintain room-temperature strength.
The compositional modification will maintain room-temperature ductility.
A controlled precipitate volume fraction and nanometric precipitate size will preserve room-temperature strength and ductility.
Adding the lightweight element will leave the density similar to or slightly below that of the baseline.
The beneficial effect exists only within a narrow compositional window.
Excessive addition of the lightweight element may form coarse or brittle secondary phases that reduce room-temperature ductility or toughness.
Prior Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti studies provide an analogous example of lightweight, L21-containing precipitation-strengthened alloys tested in compression up to 700 °C.
